PASSO 1: para dizer o que se faz numa fe: STEP 1: to say what people do at a festival without saying who, use «se» + verb in the 3rd person (lesson 49): «Se celebra en marzo.» (It's celebrated in March.), «Se comen dulces típicos.» (People eat traditional sweets.) STEP 2: the verb agrees with what is celebrated or eaten: «Se celebra la fiesta» (singular), «Se celebran las fallas» (plural). STEP 3: for habits, use «soler» + infinitive, meaning "to usually do": «Suelo ir a casa de mi abuela.» (I usually go to my grandmother's.), «En Navidad solemos cenar en familia.» English has no verb for this; Spanish does. STEP 4: «soler» is irregular in the present: the stem «o» becomes «ue» (suelo, sueles, suele, solemos, soléis, suelen), like «poder». In the imperfect it's regular and expresses a past habit, like English "used to": «Solía viajar en verano.» (I used to travel in summer.) STEP 5: «soler» is always followed directly by an infinitive, with no preposition: «Suelo ir», not «Suelo a ir». STEP 6: «fiesta» is a party or festival, but also a public holiday: «día festivo». The verb «celebrar» means to celebrate and also to hold an event: «El festival se celebra en julio.» (The festival is held in July.) STEP 7: combine them to describe: «En esta fiesta se suele comer…», «La gente suele disfrazarse.»
em português dizemos «costumo ir» e «com: English says "I usually go" or "I used to go"; Spanish has a verb for it: «suelo ir», «solía ir». English "it's celebrated in March" / "people celebrate it in March" both become «se celebra en marzo». And «soler» never takes a preposition: «suelo ir», not «suelo a ir».

Um calendário de festas e como felicitar: A festival calendar and how to congratulate people
PASSO 1: conheça algumas festas. Não é n: STEP 1: get to know some festivals. You don't need to memorise everything; it's a basis for conversation. STEP 2: for set dates, use short formulas: «¡Feliz Navidad!», «¡Feliz Año Nuevo!», «¡Felices fiestas!» (Happy holidays!), «¡Feliz cumpleaños!». STEP 3: for an achievement (passing an exam, good news), use «¡Enhorabuena!» (Spain) or «¡Felicidades!» / «¡Felicitaciones!» (very common in Latin America). Don't use «enhorabuena» for a birthday. STEP 4: to wish someone well, use «que» + subjunctive, with the verb right after: «Que lo pases bien.» (Have a good time.), «Que disfrutes de las fiestas.», «Que tengas un buen viaje.» (Have a good trip.) It's the same subjunctive of wishing from lesson 43. STEP 5: «Ojalá» also expresses a wish and takes the subjunctive: «Ojalá haga buen tiempo.» (I hope the weather's good.) STEP 6: the date of a festival takes the article and no preposition: «El 6 de enero», «el último miércoles de agosto», «el uno y el dos de noviembre» — English "ON 6 January" has no equivalent preposition.

And beware: «aniversario» is only an anniversary (of a wedding, an event); a birthday is «cumpleaños».

Comparar costumes e contar como eram: Comparing customs and saying how things used to be
PASSO 1: para contrastar, use «mientras: STEP 1: to contrast, use «mientras que» (while, whereas): «En Estados Unidos se cena pronto, mientras que en España se cena más tarde.» STEP 2: «a diferencia de» + noun (unlike): «A diferencia de Estados Unidos, en España…». STEP 3: for similarities: «igual que», «como» and «se parece a»: «Se parece a nuestro Halloween.» (the verb is «parecerse a»). STEP 4: to say how customs used to be, use the habitual imperfect (lesson 21) or «solía»: «Cuando era pequeña, mi familia se reunía en Navidad.» (When I was little, my family used to get together at Christmas.), «Antes se solía celebrar en casa; ahora se hace en la calle.» STEP 5: with dates, never use a preposition: «Se celebra el último miércoles de agosto.»

— Camila, como se comemora o Ano Novo no: — Camila, how do you celebrate New Year's Eve in Mexico? Here we eat twelve grapes with the chimes.
— Em muitas casas também se comem as uva: — In lots of homes people eat the grapes too, but the most important thing is having dinner with the family and making a toast.
— E o Dia dos Mortos? Vi fotos de altare: — And the Day of the Dead? I've seen photos of really beautiful altars.
— Comemora-se no dia primeiro e no dia d: — It's celebrated on the first and second of November. People put photos of family members who have passed away, flowers and food on an altar.

Nochevieja y las doce uvas / A virada do: Nochevieja y las doce uvas / New Year's Eve and the twelve grapes
Na Espanha, a noite de 31 de dezembro se: In Spain, the night of 31 December is called Nochevieja. Many families have dinner together and, before midnight, turn on the TV to follow the chimes of the clock. With each chime you eat a grape: twelve in total. It isn't easy, because you have to eat them fast, so many people prepare them beforehand, without seeds. Then everyone makes a toast, wishes each other «¡Feliz Año Nuevo!» and hugs. It's said that this custom brings good luck for the year ahead. Some people go out dancing afterwards and others prefer to stay at home.
